## The Big Picture: What We Built & How It Works

Today’s change set is centered on turning a mostly static publishing and automation setup into something that remembers more, reports more, and runs with less manual intervention. The main repository activity came from `kprsnt.in`, where a large auto-update commit touched workflow files, environment examples, and agent instructions. That strongly suggests the engineering focus was not just content updates, but infrastructure: daily job orchestration, shared agent behavior, and telemetry around those jobs.

The real bottleneck this addresses is operational drift. In systems like this, the failure mode is usually not one big crash — it is small inconsistencies: workflows that run but do not leave enough trace, agent jobs that lose prior context, or daily summaries that are generated without a stable memory layer. By expanding swarm memory and daily views, the system can preserve state across runs instead of treating each execution as isolated. Adding telemetry closes the loop: it makes the automation measurable, which is what lets you debug missed jobs, slow steps, or broken handoffs without guessing.

Architecturally, this is the difference between a set of independent scripts and a coordinated pipeline. The updated workflows and agent instructions imply a more opinionated execution model: jobs are scheduled by GitHub Actions, agents operate under shared rules, and telemetry records what happened so the next run can continue from a known state. That reduces manual recovery work and makes the whole publishing/automation stack easier to trust.
